recent_posts.title: KDE Plasma 6.7 To Provide A Much Better Experience For CPU-Based Rendering
recent_posts.summary: KDE Plasma 6.7 will significantly improve CPU-based rendering performance in KWin by using Linux's UDMABUF to wrap MEMFD-allocated memory into DMA-BUF objects, eliminating costly texture upload copies to the GPU. Previously, Wayland shared memory (wl_shm) buffers required excess copies before reaching the GPU, causing KWin's main thread to block and spike CPU usage. With the fix, KWin will attempt to create a UDMABUF for each wl_shm buffer and import it directly into the GPU driver. Real-world results on a Ryzen 7840U show KWin CPU usage during scrolling dropped from 80-90% on one core to just 20%, with cursor smoothness fully restored. The improvement will ship in Plasma 6.7 and Qt 6.11.2.

recent_posts.title: New GCC Back-End Proposed For WebAssembly
recent_posts.summary: A new GCC back-end for WebAssembly has been proposed via a patch series on the GCC mailing list. Currently around 3,000 lines of code and marked as a request for comments, the back-end is in early development and lacks features like WASM reference types, exceptions, and debug info. This is the first significant WASM activity for GCC in years, potentially offering an alternative to the dominant LLVM/Clang-based WebAssembly toolchain. It still awaits approval from the GCC Steering Committee.

recent_posts.title: Rust-Written Redox OS Sees Improvements For Running On Real Hardware
recent_posts.summary: Redox OS, the Rust-written operating system, published its April 2026 status report highlighting improvements for running on real hardware. Key updates include boot fixes, updated ACPI crate support for broader hardware compatibility, reduced boot times on multi-core systems, RISC-V hardware improvements, a tmux port, better CPU time stats, and improved Orbital desktop performance via partial window pixel updates. Kernel-level fixes address memory leaks, multi-threading stability, and potential deadlocks. The Bochs video driver was replaced by the VESA driver, and the Relibc libc implementation received several enhancements.

recent_posts.title: AMD Expands ROCm Support On Windows WSL To More Ryzen Hardware
recent_posts.summary: AMD has released librocdxg 1.2, expanding ROCm support on Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) to more Ryzen hardware. The update adds official support for GFX11.0.3 (Radeon 780M integrated graphics) and GFX11.5.2 (RDNA 3.5, used in Krackan Point APUs). This ROCDXG-based solution improves ROCm GPU compute and AI stack compatibility within WSL2 on Windows 11, replacing the older legacy WSL support approach. The release follows AMD ROCm 7.2.3 by just two days.

recent_posts.title: NVIDIA Looking To Create New Tool For Generating AutoFDO Profiles For GCC
recent_posts.summary: NVIDIA compiler engineers are proposing a new standalone tool for generating AutoFDO profiles specifically for GCC. The motivation is that existing AutoFDO tooling from Google is tailored for LLVM/Clang, leaving GCC without a proper profile creation workflow. The proposed tool aims to be lightweight, memory-efficient, and well-integrated with the GNU toolchain. A request for comments has been posted to the GCC mailing list by NVIDIA engineer Kugan Vivekanandarajah. AutoFDO can yield significant performance gains by allowing the compiler to use runtime sampling profiles to guide optimizations during secondary builds.

recent_posts.title: ROCm 7.2.3 Brings Minor Updates, ROCm XIO Documentation
recent_posts.summary: ROCm 7.2.3 has been released less than a month after 7.2.2, bringing minor improvements to AMD's open-source GPU compute and AI stack. Key changes include improved profiling accuracy for vLLM workloads (fixing large sporadic idle gaps), MIGraphX performance gains for the gather operator, and better ONNX Runtime reliability. Notably, the release adds documentation for ROCm XIO, an API enabling direct I/O from AMD GPU accelerators to NVMe SSDs, RDMA NICs, and SDMA engines without host processor involvement. ROCm XIO was quietly launched in April as an early-access technology preview. No new hardware or OS support changes are included; Ubuntu 26.04 LTS support is expected in ROCm 7.3.

recent_posts.title: Valve's Steam Controller Now Shipping
recent_posts.summary: Valve's new Steam Controller is now shipping at $99 USD, following its announcement alongside the Steam Frame and new Steam Machine. The controller features magnetic thumbsticks, 4 haptic motors, an 8.39 Wh battery, and supports both wireless and wired operation. On Linux, it works through the Steam Runtime, though no dedicated HID kernel driver patches have appeared outside of Steam yet. US delivery is estimated at 3–5 business days.

recent_posts.title: Omarchy 3.7 Linux Distribution Overhauls Gaming Support, Adds Unified CLI
recent_posts.summary: Omarchy 3.7, the Arch Linux-based desktop distribution using the Hyprland compositor and led by DHH, has been released with major updates. Gaming support has been overhauled to include a streamlined Steam installer, pre-configured RetroArch, improved controller handling, and better integration with Lutris, Heroic, and Moonlight GameStream. An Xbox Cloud Gaming web app option is also added. A new unified 'omarchy' CLI command replaces the previous fragmented 'omarchy-*' commands, offering tab completion and helpers for issue analysis, software installation, and screenshots. Other additions include built-in OCR-based text extraction via Tesseract, the cliamp text-based music player shipped by default, Intel FRED support for Panther Lake systems, and improved ASUS ExpertBook Panther Lake laptop support.

recent_posts.title: GCC 16 Compiler Delivering Some Decent Performance Gains Over GCC 15
recent_posts.summary: GCC 16.1, the first stable feature release of GCC 16, shows measurable performance gains over GCC 15. Initial benchmarks were run on Fedora Workstation 44 using an HP Z6 G5 A workstation with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9975WX (Zen 5) processor, 128GB DDR5-5600 RAM, and 1TB NVMe SSD. Tests used -O3 -march=native build flags. GCC 16 brings notable changes including AMD Zen 6 and Arm AGI CPU support, new C++ features, and an Algol 68 language front-end. More benchmarks across additional hardware and a GCC 16 vs. LLVM/Clang comparison are forthcoming.

recent_posts.title: CachyOS Switches Python To Using Tail-Call Interpreter For 5~15% Better Performance
recent_posts.summary: CachyOS has updated its Python package to use the new tail-call interpreter introduced in Python 3.14, delivering a 5–15% performance improvement when built with a compatible compiler like GCC 16. The change is automatic for users who upgrade to the latest CachyOS packages, requiring no manual configuration. The tail-call interpreter was originally merged into CPython via a pull request last year and officially debuted as an option in Python 3.14.
